recipe.history:
Chives are among the most ancient and widely distributed of all the allium family, growing wild across a remarkable sweep of the northern hemisphere from Siberia to northern China to the alpine meadows of Europe. Their cultivation is documented in Chinese records going back over four thousand years, and they appear in the writings of Marco Polo as one of the things he encountered and admired in the gardens he passed through on his travels. Unlike their larger allium cousins — onion, garlic, leek — chives offer a gentler, more refined flavor, a bright green grassiness with just enough onion heat to make itself known without overwhelming. They were cultivated in European monastery gardens through the Middle Ages and became essential to French fine cuisine, particularly as a component of the classic fines herbes blend alongside parsley, tarragon, and chervil. The pear, meanwhile, has its own ancient lineage — Pliny the Elder catalogued over forty varieties in Roman times, and the fruit has been a staple of European orchards for millennia, prized for its yielding sweetness and delicate floral perfume.

In American cooking, chive cream became a natural accompaniment for richer, beefier preparations once French-influenced cuisine filtered into the mainstream in the latter half of the twentieth century. The lightness of crème fraîche or sour cream tempered with chives provided acid and brightness against the fat of ground beef, and the combination found its way into steakhouse sauces and burger toppings through the 1980s and 1990s. Mostarda — the Italian condiment of candied fruit suspended in a pungent mustard syrup — was a revelation when it arrived in American specialty food culture, offering something fundamentally different from any familiar condiment: fruit that is simultaneously sweet, hot, and acidic. Pear mostarda in particular, with its gentle sweetness and slightly grainy texture, pairs with beef in a way that feels both unexpected and inevitable, the fruit's natural sugars caramelizing slightly against the heat of the patty.

I first made pear mostarda on a grey November afternoon when I had too many pears going soft on the counter and a jar of dry mustard powder that I had bought for some project I had forgotten. I simmered the pears down with white wine and sugar and mustard seeds, and the result filled the kitchen with a smell that was warm and sweet and just slightly eye-watering — that particular mustard sharpness that catches in the back of your throat. I put it on a burger that evening almost as an afterthought, along with a smear of chive cream I had left over from a weekend brunch, and understood immediately that the two things belonged together with beef. The chive cream is cool and herby and subtly sharp; the mostarda is warm and sweet and hot. Between them, the medium rare patty is the most important element, the hinge that the two condiments rotate around.

The philosophy of medium rare is, at its core, a philosophy of restraint — of knowing when to stop, of respecting the material you are working with enough not to destroy it. Ground beef at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is still expressing itself, still communicating what it is and where it came from. The fat has begun to render but has not been driven entirely from the muscle fibers; the proteins have set but not contracted into something that can only be chewed, not tasted. A medium rare burger is a burger that has been cooked with intention and removed from heat with confidence. A well-done burger is a burger that someone was afraid of. Pair it with chive cream and pear mostarda and you have a burger that demands to be eaten slowly, and a medium rare patty is the only one worth slowing down for.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
2 firm Bosc pears, peeled, cored, and cut into 1/2-inch dice
3 tbsp fresh chives, very finely sliced, plus more for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the pear mostarda: Combine pears, white wine, white wine vinegar, sugar, mustard seeds, dry mustard, salt, and white pepper in a medium saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, for 25–30 minutes until the liquid has reduced to a thick, glossy syrup and the pear pieces are translucent but still hold their shape. Remove from heat and let cool to room temperature. The mostarda can be made up to 1 week ahead and stored refrigerated.

2. Make the chive cream: Whisk together crème fraîche, sour cream, chives, lemon juice, lemon zest, salt, and white pepper in a small bowl until smooth and combined. Taste and adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until ready to use.

3. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg and mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.
5. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape each into a smooth ball, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and let rise again until doubled and puffy, about 45 minutes.
6. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns with egg wash and bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

7. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions of about 170g each. Form gently into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
9. Lay a slice of white cheddar on each patty. Add a splash of water, cover with a lid, and steam 30–45 seconds until melted.
10. Transfer patties to a resting rack and rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
11. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

12. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of chive cream on the bottom bun. Place the cheesed patty on top. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of pear mostarda over the patty. Add a small handful of watercress. Scatter a few extra sliced chives over the top. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately.
